text: Windows whose ends only move forward; pairs from both ends.
l rboth only move right
Two pointers (双指针): keep a window [l, r] and move both ends only forward.

Each pointer travels at most n steps, so the whole scan is O(n), even though it looks at "all windows". It works when moving r forward can only make the window "more" (bigger sum, more kinds) and moving l forward can only make it "less".

Same-direction pointers handle "shortest / longest window with a property". Opposite-direction pointers (one at each end of a sorted array, moving inward) handle "pairs with a given sum or difference".

For each right end r, the shortest good window ends at r and starts at the largest l that still keeps every painter. That l never moves back when r grows, so l and r together move at most 2n times (P1638). Keep a cnt[] array and a kinds counter so each step is O(1).

Longest window without repeats (UVA11572) shrinks only when the new value is already inside. Counting pairs with a − b = c (P1102) after sorting: as a[i] grows, the block of values equal to a[i] + c only moves right, so two pointers replace the binary searches of 第13章 . Diamond Collector (P3143) and Sure Bet (P4653) are two-pointer scans on sorted data.
Store running values and counts so each step is O(1).

Space for time (空间换时间): store results you would otherwise recompute, such as a running total, a prefix minimum or a count per value, so each step reads them in O(1). The cost is memory, which is usually plentiful compared with time.

Checking all O(n²) subarrays is too slow for n = 2 × 10⁵. Keep only one stored value: the best sum of a subarray ending at the current position. It either extends the previous best or starts fresh, whichever is larger (P1115).
The same answer comes from prefix sums: best = max over r of (S[r] − min S[l] for l < r), with the minimum stored as you go. One stored number replaces a whole inner loop.

Re-sorting after every new score costs O(n log n) each time. Scores are only 0 … 600, so store a count per score and walk down from 600 until enough winners are covered: at most 601 steps per player (P7072).

When values come from a small range, a counting array (基础篇第5章) is the "space" that buys the time. Grouping indices by colour and parity before pairing them up (P2671) is the same idea with sums stored per group.
Nearest greater / smaller elements; largest rectangles.
stack keeps decreasing heights

A monotonic stack (单调栈) keeps its contents sorted, for example decreasing from bottom to top. Before pushing x, pop everything that x "beats". Each element is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n) in total.
At the moment an element is popped, the element causing the pop is its next greater (or smaller) element to the right. What remains below it in the stack is its nearest greater element to the left.

Count, for every cow, how many cows to its right it can see over. Turn it around: when cow i arrives, the cows that can see it are exactly the taller ones still in a decreasing stack. Shorter or equal ones are popped forever, since cow i blocks their view (P2866).
R F F F F F F F F F F F R R R F F F F F F F F F F F F F F F

Largest rectangle of F cells: for every row, h[j] is how many F cells stand in column j ending at this row. The best rectangle with height h[j] stretches left and right until the first lower column, found for all j with two monotonic-stack passes: O(nm) overall (P4147). Counting all rectangles (P1950) and the poster problem (P3467) use the same "nearest lower" arrays.
Sliding-window minimum and maximum with a deque.
w [2, 4]: deque keeps indices 3, 4 (values increasing); front = mi

A monotonic queue (单调队列) finds the minimum (or maximum) of every window of length k in O(n) total. Keep a deque of indices whose values increase from front to back: a new value pops every bigger value from the back, because those can never be a window minimum again; the front leaves when it falls out of the window.
The front of the deque is always the minimum of the current window. Each index enters and leaves once.

Best sum of at most m consecutive pieces: with prefix sums, the sum of (l, r] is S[r] − S[l], so for each r we want the smallest S[l] with r − m ≤ l < r: a sliding-window minimum over the prefix sums (P1714).

Window maximum (P2032), the max − min of every k × k square by running the queue on rows and then on columns (P2216), and recurrences like "best of the last k states" (P1725) all reuse this deque. Range max/min with arbitrary queries (P2880) needs a sparse table (第3章).
